name: Pedong
tagline: Last bazaar before Jelep La, with a Lepcha fort above it
meta_description: Pedong, 20 km from Kalimpong: Damsang fort ruins, Sangchen Dorjee monastery, Cross Hill, the old Tibet trade road, jeeps, homestays and real costs.
summary: Pedong is a small bazaar town at 1,240 m, 20 km east of Kalimpong, on the old trade road to Tibet over Jelep La. It has three layers of history within a few kilometres: the Lepcha fort of Damsang, the Bhutanese-era Sangchen Dorjee monastery and the French mission's Cross Hill. A day trip or one night.

local_story.title: Fort, monastery and mission on the Tibet road
paras: Pedong's history starts above the town at Damsang. In the late 17th century the Lepcha chief Gaeboo Achyok ruled a principality from here and fought the Drukpas of Bhutan for these hills. The fort usually dated to 1690, Damsang Gadi, was his stronghold; Lepcha lore says spirits carried its smooth round stones up from the Reshi river. Achyok was eventually captured and executed, Bhutan took the hills, and the fort was later used against the British before falling into ruin after the war of 1864.

Under Bhutanese rule, in the early 1700s, the Sangchen Dorjee monastery was built at Pedong, in the Drukpa Kagyu tradition of Bhutan. After the Treaty of Sinchula in 1865 the area passed to British India, and Pedong became a stage on the Kalimpong–Lhasa trade road. Mule caravans laden with Tibetan wool came down from Jelep La through Rhenock and Pedong, until the 1962 war closed the pass.

The road also drew missionaries hoping to reach Tibet. In 1882 the French priest Auguste Desgodins, of the Paris Foreign Missions, set up Cross Hill above Pedong as a memorial to missionaries who had died or disappeared trying to enter Tibet. It remains a place of pilgrimage for local Catholics.

did_you_know: Every 20 December, Lepchas from Kalimpong, Darjeeling and Sikkim gather at Damsang fort to mark the birth anniversary of the Lepcha chief Gaeboo Achyok.
Sangchen Dorjee monastery at Pedong was built in the early 1700s under Bhutanese rule and follows the Drukpa Kagyu tradition, Bhutan's state school of Buddhism.
Cross Hill above Pedong was erected in 1882 by Fr Auguste Desgodins as a memorial to missionaries who died or disappeared trying to reach Tibet.
intro: Pedong is not pretty in the postcard sense: a ridge-top bazaar of concrete shops, a jeep stand and a few lanes. But it sits at a crossroads of history, and within a short drive you can stand in a 17th-century Lepcha fort, a Bhutanese monastery and a 19th-century French mission site. It is also the jumping-off point for Sillery Gaon, Icchey Gaon, Ramitey Dara and the road into Sikkim at Reshi.

Most people see Pedong on a day trip from Kalimpong or on the way to Sillery Gaon. A night here is cheap, with simple lodges and homestays around the town, and the evening bazaar is a real local market rather than a tourist one. Shared jeeps run from Kalimpong in about an hour.
facts: Damsang fort, Sangchen Dorjee, Cross Hill, trade-route history
costs: Thali or momos in the bazaar

highlights.title: Damsang fort ruins
highlights.text: The ruined stronghold of the Lepcha chief Gaeboo Achyok on a forested ridge above Pedong, usually dated to 1690. Low walls and scattered stones, wide views and a story that matters deeply to the Lepcha community.

highlights.title: Sangchen Dorjee monastery
highlights.text: Built in the early 1700s under Bhutanese rule, in the Drukpa Kagyu tradition. Old wall paintings and a quiet courtyard just outside the town. Ask before photographing inside.

highlights.title: Cross Hill
highlights.text: A hilltop cross raised in 1882 by the French missionary Auguste Desgodins as a memorial to those who died trying to reach Tibet. A short climb, with views over the Rishi valley into Sikkim.

highlights.title: The old Tibet road
highlights.text: Pedong was a stage on the mule road from Kalimpong to Jelep La and Lhasa. Ask older residents about the caravans that passed before 1962; some families' shops date from that trade.

highlights.title: Gateway to Sillery Gaon
highlights.text: Sillery Gaon, Icchey Gaon and the Ramitey Dara viewpoint are a short drive from Pedong, and the road to Reshi leads into East Sikkim towards Aritar and Rongli.

how_to_reach.text: Shared jeeps leave Kalimpong's Motor Stand for Pedong through the morning and early afternoon, ₹80–120 a seat, about an hour via Algarah. The last jeeps back leave Pedong by mid-afternoon.

From Kalimpong, a car costs ₹1,500–2,200 one way, or ₹2,500–3,500 for a half-day package covering Damsang, Sangchen Dorjee and Cross Hill. From NJP or Bagdogra, about ₹4,500–5,500 and 3.5–4.5 hours; NH10 has had closures since October 2023, so check current status before you travel.
Pedong is about 30 km from Aritar in East Sikkim via Rhenock and the Reshi bridge, 1.5 hours by car. Foreign nationals need a Sikkim permit arranged in advance.

where_to_stay: Pedong has a few simple lodges and family homestays around the bazaar and on the roads leading out, at about ₹1,200–1,800 per person with meals; they are functional rather than scenic. For views and a village feel, most travellers sleep in Sillery Gaon, 5–6 km above, or Icchey Gaon, and visit Pedong for its history. If you want a heritage or government lodge, stay in Kalimpong at Morgan House or the Tashiding Tourist Lodge and do Pedong as a day trip.
tips: Start from Kalimpong by 9 am to see Damsang, the monastery and Cross Hill before afternoon cloud.
Wear walking shoes for Damsang, where the last stretch is a rough forest path.
Visit on 20 December if you want to see the Lepcha gathering at Damsang fort.
Check the time of the last shared jeep back to Kalimpong when you arrive.
Roads around Pedong and Reshi can be blocked by landslides in the monsoon: check current status before you travel.

experiences.title: Damsang, the Lepcha fort above Pedong
experiences.summary: Walk to the ruins of Damsang Gadi, the 17th-century stronghold of the Lepcha chief Gaeboo Achyok, on a forested ridge above Pedong. Low stone walls, wide views and the founding story of Lepcha resistance.
body: Damsang is the most important historic site of the Lepcha people in the Kalimpong hills. In the second half of the 17th century, Gaeboo Achyok led a Lepcha principality from here and fought to keep the hills from the expanding kingdom of Bhutan, allying with Tibet. The fort, Damsang Gadi, is usually dated to 1690, though historians differ on the exact years of his rule. He was captured and executed, and Bhutan held the hills until 1865.

Lepcha lore says the fort was built with the help of spirits, who carried large, smooth round stones up from the Reshi river; take that as a cherished story. The fort was used again against the British East India Company, and fell into ruin after the Anglo-Bhutan war of 1864. Today you see low walls and scattered dressed stones among trees, on a ridge with views towards Sikkim.

A local car from Pedong to the nearest road point costs about ₹600–1,000 return, followed by a 15–30 minute walk on a forest path. You can also walk from Pedong, Sillery Gaon or Icchey Gaon with a guide. Do not climb on the walls. On 20 December, Lepchas gather here for Achyok's birth anniversary.

faqs.q: Who built Damsang fort?
faqs.a: Damsang fort was the stronghold of the Lepcha chief Gaeboo Achyok, who ruled a principality based here in the late 17th century and fought Bhutanese expansion. It is usually dated to 1690. Lepcha lore says spirits helped carry its stones from the Reshi river.

faqs.q: How do I reach Damsang fort?
faqs.a: From Pedong, take a local car to the nearest road point, about ₹600–1,000 return, then walk 15–30 minutes on a forest path. It is about 6 km from Icchey Gaon, and a good half-day walk with a guide from Pedong or Sillery Gaon.

faqs.q: What is left of Damsang fort today?
faqs.a: Only ruins: low stone walls and scattered dressed stones on a forested hilltop. The fort fell to ruin after the Anglo-Bhutan war of 1864. Go for the history, the Lepcha story and the views, not for a standing castle.

experiences.title: Sangchen Dorjee, Pedong's Bhutanese monastery
experiences.summary: Visit the monastery built at Pedong in the early 1700s, when the Kalimpong hills were part of Bhutan. Drukpa Kagyu, the state school of Bhutan, with old murals and a quiet courtyard.
body: When Bhutan ruled the hills east of the Teesta, from the early 18th century until 1865, it built monasteries to anchor its authority. Sangchen Dorjee at Pedong is one of them, founded in the early 1700s. It follows the Drukpa Kagyu tradition, the school of Tibetan Buddhism that is the state religion of Bhutan, which makes it different from most of the Tibetan monasteries in Kalimpong town.

The building has been repaired and rebuilt over three centuries, but the setting and the atmosphere are old. Look for the wall paintings of Tantric deities and protectors inside the prayer hall, and the prayer wheels in the courtyard. Visitors are welcome outside ritual times; ask a monk or caretaker before entering and before taking photographs.
It is a short walk or drive from Pedong bazaar. Combine it with Damsang fort and Cross Hill for a half day of three eras of Pedong history. Dress modestly, walk clockwise and leave a small donation.

faqs.q: How old is Sangchen Dorjee monastery?
faqs.a: It was founded in the early 1700s, during Bhutanese rule of the Kalimpong hills, which makes it one of the oldest monasteries in the area. It has been repaired and rebuilt over the centuries. It follows the Drukpa Kagyu tradition of Bhutan.

faqs.q: Is Sangchen Dorjee monastery open to visitors?
faqs.a: Yes, generally during the day outside ritual times. Ask a monk or caretaker before entering the prayer hall and before taking photographs. There is no entry fee; a small donation is welcome. Timings can change on festival days.

faqs.q: Is Pedong monastery different from Kalimpong's monasteries?
faqs.a: Yes. Sangchen Dorjee follows Bhutan's Drukpa Kagyu tradition and dates from the Bhutanese period. Most of Kalimpong town's monasteries, such as Zang Dhok Palri, were founded or rebuilt by Tibetan lamas, especially after 1959, in other schools.

experiences.title: Cross Hill and the missionaries of the Tibet road
experiences.summary: Climb to Cross Hill, where the French missionary Auguste Desgodins raised a cross in 1882 to remember those who died or disappeared trying to reach Tibet. Views over the Rishi valley and a quiet chapter of the trade road's story.
body: In the 19th century Tibet was closed to most outsiders, and Catholic missionaries of the Paris Foreign Missions spent decades on its borders, trying to enter from China and from India. Several died or vanished on the way. Pedong, on the trade road to Jelep La, was as close as many of them could get.

In 1882 Fr Auguste Desgodins, a French missionary who had spent years on the Tibetan frontier, set up a Catholic mission at Pedong and raised a cross on the hill above the town as a memorial to those who had died or disappeared trying to reach Tibet. Cross Hill is still a pilgrimage site for local Catholics, and the Catholic presence in Pedong dates from that mission.

The climb is short. At the top, the view runs over the Rishi valley and the border into Sikkim, along the line the caravans took. Be respectful: it is a religious site. Combine it with Sangchen Dorjee monastery and Damsang fort for a half day.

faqs.q: What is Cross Hill in Pedong?
faqs.a: Cross Hill is a hilltop above Pedong where the French missionary Fr Auguste Desgodins raised a cross in 1882 as a memorial to missionaries who died or disappeared trying to reach Tibet. It is a pilgrimage site for local Catholics and a viewpoint over the Rishi valley.

faqs.q: Why were missionaries in Pedong?
faqs.a: Pedong was on the trade road from Kalimpong to Tibet over Jelep La. In the 19th century Tibet was closed to foreigners, so Catholic missionaries of the Paris Foreign Missions settled at border points like Pedong, hoping to enter. Fr Desgodins set up the Pedong mission in 1882.

faqs.q: How long does Cross Hill take?
faqs.a: About an hour including the short climb and time at the top. It is close to Pedong town and can be combined with Sangchen Dorjee monastery and Damsang fort in a half-day trip of about 3–4 hours.

experiences.title: Pedong bazaar and the old mule road
experiences.summary: Wander Pedong's bazaar in the late afternoon and look for traces of the trade that once came down from Tibet over Jelep La: old shopfronts, family businesses and elders who remember the mule caravans.
body: Until 1962, Pedong was a stage on the road that carried Tibetan wool down to Kalimpong, India's main market for it. Mule caravans came over Jelep La, through the Chumbi valley side, down through Rhenock and Pedong, and on to Kalimpong. Grain, cloth, sugar, kerosene and manufactured goods went the other way. The 1962 war closed the pass, and the trade stopped almost overnight.

Today the bazaar is an ordinary hill market of jeeps, hardware shops, grocers and tea stalls. But ask around, politely, and some families will tell you their shops or houses date from the trading days, or that a grandfather worked with the caravans. These are personal memories, shared on the families' terms; do not press.

Late afternoon is a good time, when villagers come in to shop and the jeeps fill for the ride home. Eat a plate of momos or a thali for ₹80–200, buy local cardamom or churpi, and watch the light fade over the Sikkim hills.

faqs.q: Was Pedong on the Silk Route?
faqs.a: Pedong was on the Kalimpong–Lhasa trade road over Jelep La, which carried Tibetan wool until 1962. Travellers often call the whole network the Silk Route. The popular Silk Route drive today runs through Rongli and Zuluk in East Sikkim, across the Rishi river from Pedong.

faqs.q: What was traded through Pedong?
faqs.a: Mainly Tibetan wool coming south to Kalimpong, India's chief market for it, along with other Tibetan goods. Northbound mules carried grain, cloth, sugar, kerosene and factory goods. The trade ended when Jelep La was closed after the 1962 war.

faqs.q: Is Jelep La open today?
faqs.a: No. Jelep La, on the Sikkim–Tibet border, has been closed to trade and travel since 1962. Limited border trade with Tibet reopened through Nathu La in 2006. Visitors can go to Nathu La from Gangtok with permits, but not to Jelep La.

faqs.q: How far is Pedong from Kalimpong?
faqs.a: About 20 km east, roughly an hour by shared jeep (₹80–120 a seat) or 45 minutes to an hour by car (₹1,500–2,200 one way). Jeeps leave from the Kalimpong Motor Stand through the morning and early afternoon.

faqs.q: What is Pedong famous for?
faqs.a: Pedong is known for Damsang fort, the 17th-century stronghold of the Lepcha chief Gaeboo Achyok; Sangchen Dorjee monastery, built under Bhutanese rule in the early 1700s; Cross Hill, raised in 1882 by a French missionary; and its place on the old Kalimpong–Tibet trade road.

faqs.q: Is Pedong worth visiting?
faqs.a: Yes, for history. In a half day you can see a Lepcha fort, a Bhutanese monastery and a French mission site, each telling part of the hills' story. Pedong itself is a plain bazaar, so most people stay in Sillery Gaon or Kalimpong and visit for the day.

faqs.q: Can I do Pedong and Sillery Gaon in one day?
faqs.a: Yes, by reserved car from Kalimpong: Pedong's sights in the morning, lunch in the bazaar, then Sillery Gaon and Ramitey Dara in the afternoon, back by evening. It is a long day; we prefer a night in Sillery Gaon for the dawn.

faqs.q: Where should I stay near Pedong?
faqs.a: For views and quiet, stay in Sillery Gaon or Icchey Gaon homestays, a short drive away. Pedong has simple lodges and homestays at about ₹1,200–1,800 per person with meals, handy for an early jeep. For heritage stays, use Kalimpong.

faqs.q: What is the best time to visit Pedong?
faqs.a: October to December for clear skies, and March to May for mild weather and spring flowers. 20 December brings the Lepcha gathering at Damsang fort. From June to September, rain and landslides can disrupt the roads.

faqs.q: Can I go from Pedong to Sikkim?
faqs.a: Yes. The road drops to the Reshi bridge on the Bengal–Sikkim border and climbs to Rhenock and Aritar, about 30 km and 1.5 hours. Indian visitors need only an ID; foreign nationals need a Sikkim Restricted Area Permit arranged in advance. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Is there a festival at Pedong?
faqs.a: The best-known is the 20 December gathering at Damsang fort, when Lepchas from across the region mark the birth anniversary of Gaeboo Achyok. The monastery also holds rituals on Buddhist dates. Ask locally for the year's programme and check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Is Pedong safe for solo travellers?
faqs.a: Yes, it is a quiet, friendly market town. Take normal care, walk to Damsang and Cross Hill in daylight, and check the time of the last jeep back to Kalimpong, usually mid-afternoon, so you are not stranded.
